title: It can rise
hookLine: Seneca on the burned city of Lyon: cities, and people, can rise again (Letters 91)

lines: A CITY IN GAUL HAS BURNED.
cards: Word arrives from far away, and there is nothing anyone can do but read it. A city in Gaul, the colony the Romans called Lugdunum, the place we call Lyon, has burned.
A man named Liberalis, who has ties to the city, is crushed. His friend Seneca, the Stoic writer, hears about it, and sits down to write a letter to another friend, Lucilius.
It begins with Liberalis's grief, and it doesn't wave it away.

teach.h: ONE NIGHT BETWEEN A CITY AND NONE.
teach.b: First, one night. Seneca is struck by how fast it happened. In his telling, a single night stood between a great city and no city at all.
Everything a city builds slowly, a fire can take quickly. He doesn't pretend otherwise. Second, expect it.

teach.h: LET NOTHING COME AS A STRANGER.
teach.b: Seneca's advice is an old Stoic one: let the mind rehearse what could happen, so that loss, when it comes, doesn't come as a total stranger. Nothing, he says, should be unexpected by us. That can sound cold.
In the letter it reads more like a friend saying: we live in a world where things fall, and you are allowed to know that ahead of time. Third, it can rise. Here the letter turns.

Seneca reminds Lucilius that cities have been leveled before, by fire and by earthquake, and have been raised again, and that the ruin can make room for something better. He hopes the same for Lyon. Not the same city.
A city, rising. Fourth, people too. The letter moves on from the city to human lives, to bodies and their endings.
Some readers carry his turn over to a person: what falls in a life can sometimes be rebuilt, slowly, stone by stone. This is not a promise that every loss gets fixed.
Yesterday's names belong to people who can never be given their lives back, and grief like that doesn't need a happy ending. Seneca's point is narrower. Ruin is real, and so is rebuilding.
Both belong to the world. Today, after days of mourning, the second half gets its turn.

how: Some readers of the Stoics turn to Seneca's letters in hard seasons, using his practice of rehearsing possible losses in advance, and his reminder that what falls can be rebuilt.

o: a Roman emperor who rebuilt Lyon after the fire
an Epicurean poet who wrote on the fear of death
a Stoic who wrote that a burned city can rise again

games.q: what's inside Seneca's letter — tap the pairs.
p: the Roman city we call Lyon
the friend crushed by the news
between a great city and none

s: Seneca's letter 91 is about the burning of Rome
it's about Lugdunum, the city we call Lyon, in Gaul.
Seneca writes that cities have been leveled and raised again
and that ruin can make room for something better.
in the letter, Seneca tells Liberalis his grief is foolish
the letter begins with his grief and takes it seriously.

games.q: you're Seneca. your friend's city has burned in a single night. what does your letter do?
o: admits the ruin, then reminds him cities have risen again.
says the city must have deserved it.
games.why: Seneca looks straight at the loss, advises expecting such things, and turns to rebuilding: it can rise.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing in your life that has fallen down: a habit you dropped, a shelf that collapsed, a friendship gone quiet, a garden left to weeds.
Look at it honestly, as Seneca looks at Lyon, then picture the first stone going back: one text, one drawer sorted, one seed in the ground. Just the first stone, and breathe with that picture.

wordCard.voice: Seneca, writing to Lucilius about a burned city, Lyon, and the hope that what falls can be built again. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a city, rising. Ruin is real, and so is the first stone. See you tomorrow.
